label: q_main1
title: Question
head: environment

label: prop:Delta-system
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Delta-system}
Suppose given a set $X$, a positive integer $n$, and an infinite family  $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets of $X$ 
such that $|M|=n$ for all $M\in \mathcal{A}$ and the cardinal $\gamma=|\mathcal{A}|$ is regular.
Then there exists an $R\subset X$ and a $\mathcal{B}\subset \mathcal{A}$ such that $|\mathcal{B}|=\gamma$ and $A\cap B=R$ for any 
distinct $A,B\in \mathcal{B}$.
head: environment

label: cor:Delta-system
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:Delta-system}
Given a set $X$, a positive integer  $n$, and an infinite family $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets of $X$ 
such that $|M|\leq n$ for all $M\in \mathcal{A}$, 
there exists an $R\subset X$ and an infinite family $\mathcal{B}\subset \mathcal{A}$ of sets of the same 
cardinality such that $A\cap B=R$ for any distinct $A,B\in \mathcal{B}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
There exists an $m\leq n$ and a countably infinite set $\mathcal{A}'\subset\mathcal{A}$ such that $|A|=m$ for $A\in\mathcal{A}'$. 
Applying Proposition~\ref{prop:Delta-system} to $\mathcal{A}'$, we obtain the required family.
head: environment

label: rem:delta
title: Remark
head: environment

label: t1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t1}
Any $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn topological group is strongly $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn.
head: environment

label: p1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p1}
If $X$ is strongly $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn, $x\in X$, and $(U_n)_{n\in\omega}$ is a \textup(not 
necessarily decreasing\textup) sequence of open subsets of $X$ for which $x\in \bigcap_{n\in \omega} \overline{U}_n$, 
then there exist a sequence $(x_k)_{k\in\omega}$ converging to $x$ and a strictly increasing sequence 
$(n_k)_{k\in\omega}$ of nonnegative integers such that $x_k\in U_{n_k}$ for all $k\in\omega$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $W_n=\bigcup_{k\ge n} U_k$. The sequence of open sets $(W_n)_{n\in\omega}$ is decreasing, and $x\in\overline{W}_n$. Hence there is a sequence 
$(y_n)_{n\in\omega}$ converging to $x$  such that $y_n \in W_n$, i.e., $y_n\in U_{m_n}$ for some $m_n\geq n$. Choose $j_0<j_1<\dots$ so that 
$m_{j_0}<m_{j_1}<\dots$\,. Then $x_k=y_{j_k}$ and $n_k=m_{j_k}$  are as required.
head: environment

label: def-absorb
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def-absorb}
We say that a family $\mathscr F$ of subsets of $X$ \emph{absorbs convergent sequences} in $X$ if, for 
every convergent sequence $S=(x_n)_{n\in \omega}$ in $X$, there exists an 
$F\in \mathscr F$ such that $S \subset F$.
head: environment

label: rem:finer
title: Remark
head: environment

label: lemma:ind-limit
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $x_k\to x$ but $\{x_k:k\in\omega\}$ is contained in no $K_n$. Since every finite set is contained in 
some $K_n$, we can choose $k_0<k_1<\dots$ so that $x_{k_j}\notin K_j$. Let $x\in K_m$ and 
$A=\{x_{k_j}:j\geq m\}$. Then $x\in \overline{A}\setminus A$. On the other hand, $A\cap K_n$ 
is finite for each $n$, so that $A$ is 
closed in $Z$. This contradiction proves the lemma.
head: environment

label: prop:kfu-group-as
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:kfu-group-as}
Suppose that an increasing family $\{F_n: n\in \omega\}$ of closed subsets of a 
$\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn topological group $G$ absorbs convergent sequences in~$G$. 
Then $F_n$ is a neighborhood of the identity element $e$ of $G$ for some $n \in \omega$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose not. Then $e\in \overline{G\setminus F_n}$ for all $n\in\omega$, and the sequence of open sets $(G\setminus F_n)_{n\in\omega}$ is decreasing. By 
Theorem~\ref{t1} there exists a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\omega}$ converging to $e$ with $x_n\notin F_n$. 
This sequence is contained in no $F_n$, which is
a contradiction.
head: environment

label: prop:kfu-group-loc-precomp
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $H$ be a $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn subgroup of $G$. The sets $P_n=(F_0\cup\dots\cup F_n)\cap H$ are closed in $H$ and precompact in $G$ (and hence in $H$).
Also, the family $\{P_n: n\in\omega\}$ is increasing and absorbs convergent sequences in $H$. 
By Proposition~\ref{prop:kfu-group-as} one of the sets $P_n$ is a neighborhood of the identity in~$H$.
head: environment

label: cor:hemicompact-group
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:hemicompact-group}
Let $G$ be a topological group which is hemicompact with respect to a family $\{K_n:n\in\omega\}$. Then every 
$\varkappa$-Fr\'echet--Urysohn subgroup $H$ of $G$ is locally precompact. More precisely, $K_n\cap H$ is a 
neighborhood of the identity in $H$ for some $n$, provided that the sequence of sets $K_n$ is increasing.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every compact subset of a topological group is closed and precompact. If a sequence $(x_k)_{k\in\omega}$ converges to $x$ 
in $G$, then $\{x\}\cup\{x_k: k\in\omega\}$ is compact and hence contained in some $K_n$; thus, the family 
$\{K_n: n\in\omega\}$ absorbs convergent sequences in $G$. It remains to apply Proposition~\ref{prop:kfu-group-loc-precomp} (and, for 
the second assertion, Proposition~\ref{prop:kfu-group-as} to the increasing family $\{K_n\cap H: n\in\omega\}$, which 
absorbs convergent sequences in $H$ by Remark~\ref{rem:finer}).
head: environment

label: lfd
title: Definition
head: environment

label: rem1
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem1}
 Clearly, any subgroup of a locally finite-dimensional group is locally finite-dimensional. Note also that 
if $G$ is a locally finite-dimensional subgroup of a TVS $V$, then so is its closure 
$\overline{G}$. Indeed, let $E$ be a finite-dimensional subspace of $V$ for which $E\cap G$ is open in $G$. 
The subspace $E$ is closed in $V$~\cite[Corollary~1.5.2]{BSS2017tvs}. Take an open set $O\subset V$ such that 
$O\cap G=E\cap G$. Since $G$ is dense in $\overline{G}$, we have 
$\varnothing\ne O\cap \overline{G}\subset \overline{O\cap G}=\overline{E\cap G}\subset E\cap \overline{G}$. 
Thus, the subgroup $E\cap \overline{G}$ of $\overline{G}$ has 
nonempty interior and hence is open  in $\overline{G}$ \cite[Corollary~1.3.3]{AT}.
head: environment

label: lemma:fd-subgroup
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\varphi\colon W\to G$ be a topological isomorphism. We claim that any continuous homomorphism 
$\psi\colon \mathbb{R}\to V$ is linear, i.e., $\psi(t)=t\psi(1)$ for all $t\in \mathbb{R}$. Indeed, for $m\in\mathbb Z$ and 
 $k\in \omega\setminus\{0\}$, we have $k\psi(m/k)=\psi(m)=m\psi(1)$, whence 
$\psi(m/k)=\frac mk\psi(1)$ (we divide in the vector space $V$). Thus, the continuous maps $t\mapsto \psi(t)$ and 
$t\mapsto t\psi(1)$ coincide on $\mathbb{Q}$ and hence on $\mathbb{R}$, because $V$ is Hausdorff. 

Applying this to the continuous homomorphisms $t\mapsto \varphi(tw)$, $w\in W$, we obtain 
$\varphi(tw)=t\varphi(w)$ for all $t\in \mathbb{R}$ and $w\in W$. Hence $\varphi$ is an injective linear map, 
and $G=\varphi(W)$ is a linear subspace of $V$ of dimension $\dim W$.
head: environment

label: th:lc-subgroups
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By F.~Riesz' theorem (see \cite[Theorem~1.5.1]{BSS2017tvs}) any subspace $E$ of finite dimension $n$ in any 
TVS $V$ is topologically isomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$. Therefore, each 
of the conditions (iv)--(vi) implies (i); in the case of (iv), note that $E\cap G$ is closed in $E$ and 
hence locally compact. Clearly, (ii) and (iii) imply (i) as well. 

Suppose that condition (i) holds. Then $G$ is closed in $V$ \cite[Proposition~1.4.19]{AT}. By the vector group splitting theorem  
\cite[Theorem~7.57]{Hofmann-Morris} any locally compact abelian group $G$ can be written as the direct 
product of $E=\mathbb{R}^m$ (where $m$ is a nonnegative integer) and a locally compact group $H$ 
containing a compact open subgroup. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:fd-subgroup}\, $E$ is a finite-dimensional subspace of $V$. 
Any compact subgroup $K$ of $V$ is trivial: if $g\in K\setminus\{0\}$, then $K\cap \mathbb{R} g$ is a compact 
subgroup of the line $\mathbb{R} g\cong \mathbb{R}$ containing $g\ne 0$, which is impossible. Hence $H$ is discrete, and $H$ is 
closed in $V$, being locally compact. 
 Therefore, (i) implies (ii)--(vi).
head: environment

label: th:lfd-subgroups
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
According to Remark~\ref{rem1}, 
a subgroup $G$ of a TVS $V$ is locally finite-dimensional in $V$ if and only if 
so is its closure $\overline{G}$. Therefore, Theorem~\ref{th:lc-subgroups} implies the equivalence of 
(i)  and (ii). Clearly, (iii)  follows from~(ii).

Let us prove  that (iii) implies (i). Let $\widehat V$ be the completion of $V$, and let $H$ be the closure of $G$ 
in $\widehat V$. Being a closed subgroup of the complete group $\widehat V$, the group $H$ is complete, and $G$ 
is dense in $H$; hence $H$ is the Ra\u\i kov completion of $G$. Since $G$ is locally precompact, $H$ is locally 
compact. By Theorem~\ref{th:lc-subgroups} applied to the TVS $\widehat V$, there exists a 
finite-dimensional subspace $E$ of $\widehat V$ for which $E\cap H$ is open in $H$. Then $E\cap G$ is open in $G$, 
and $E_0=E\cap V$ is a finite-dimensional subspace of $V$ such that $E_0\cap G=E\cap G$. Thus, $G$ is locally 
finite-dimensional.
head: environment

label: prop-new
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-new}
A linear subspace $W$ of a TVS $V$ is locally finite-dimensional as a subgroup of $V$ if and only if $W$ is finite-dimensional.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If a subspace $W$ is locally finite-dimensional, then it contains an open finite-dimensional subspace and is 
therefore locally compact, because any finite-dimensional space is topologically isomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$ for 
some $n\in \omega$. It is well known that any locally compact vector space is 
finite-dimensional~\cite[Theorem~1.5.6]{BSS2017tvs}. 

The converse is obvious.
head: environment

label: prop:sg-tvs
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) Suppose that $U\subset B(r)$, where $r>0$, and $x\in U$. Let $W=U-x$. Then $W$ is a neighborhood 
of zero in $G$ and $W\subset B(2r)$.
For each  positive integer $m$, the continuity of addition in $G$ 
implies the existence of a neighborhood $W_m$ of zero in $G$ such that $m W_m\subset W$ and hence 
$W_m\subset B(2r/m)$. Since both topologies are invariant under translations, 
the topology of $G$ is finer than that generated by the norm~$\lVert\boldsymbol\cdot\rVert$.

Assertion (ii) follows from (i) because the topology of $G$ is induced from $V$ and 
is therefore coarser than the norm topology.

(iii) As shown in the proof of (i), $G$ has a neighborhood $W$ of zero with $W\subset B(s)$ for some 
$s>0$. Let $m$ be a positive integer such that $s/m\le r$, and let $W'$ be a neighborhood of zero in $G$ 
for which $m W'\subset W$. Then $W'\subset B(r)$. By assumption $B(r)$ is precompact in $V$; hence so is 
$W'$, and $W'$ is precompact in $G$ as well (see Section~\ref{Preliminaries}). 
Consequently, $G$ is locally precompact. By Theorem~\ref{th:lfd-subgroups} the group $G$ 
is locally finite-dimensional.
head: environment

label: prop:sg-baire-tvs
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In view of Proposition~\ref{prop:sg-tvs}, it suffices to show that there exists a non\-empty 
norm-bounded set $U \subset G$ open in $G$.

Let $F_n = G \cap B(n)$ for $n \in \omega$. Then all $F_n$ are closed in $G$ and 
$G = \bigcup_{n \in \omega} F_n$, so that $G$  being Baire  implies  the 
existence of an $n\in \omega$ for which the interior 
$\operatorname{Int}(B(n)\cap G)$ of $B(n)\cap G$ in $G$ is nonempty. Clearly, $U=\operatorname{Int}(B(n)\cap G)$ 
has the required properties.
head: environment

label: prop:kfu-group-tvs
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In view of Proposition~\ref{prop:sg-tvs}, it suffices to prove the existence of a non\-empty norm-bounded 
set $U \subset G$ open in~$G$.

Let $F_n=G\cap B(n)$ for $n\in\omega$.
Then the increasing family $\{F_n: n\in \omega\}$ of closed subsets of the $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn topological group $G$ absorbs convergent sequences in $G$.
According to Proposition~\ref{prop:kfu-group-as}, the interior $Int(F_n)$ of $F_n$ in $G$ is a neighborhood 
of zero in $G$ for some $n \in \omega$; clearly, it is norm-bounded.
head: environment

label: th:criterion
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first assertion follows from Propositions~\ref{prop:kfu-group-tvs}(iii) and~\ref{prop:sg-baire-tvs}(iii), and 
the second assertion follows from the first assertion and Proposition~\ref{prop-new}. If $W$ is a linear subspace of $V$ and a subgroup 
$G\subset W$ is locally finite-dimensional in $V$, i.e., $E\cap G$ is open in $G$ for a finite-dimensional 
subspace $E$ of $V$, then $E\cap W$ is a finite-dimensional subspace of $W$ and $(E\cap W)\cap G=E\cap G$.
head: environment

label: lemma:bs-as
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For any $A\subset E$, the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm (a)] $A$ is norm-bounded;
\item[\rm (b)] $A$ is weakly bounded, i.e., bounded in $E_w$;
\item[\rm (c)] $A$ is precompact in $E_w$.
\end{enumerate}
The implication (a)$\implies$(b) is obvious, and (b)$\Longleftrightarrow$(c) was noted earlier in Section \ref{Preliminaries}. Let us prove 
(b)$\implies$(a). The dual $E'$ of $E$ is a Banach space, and the canonical embedding $E\to E''$ is an 
isometry. If $A$ is weakly bounded, then the family of functionals $\{\varphi\mapsto\varphi(x): x\in A\}$ on 
the Banach space $E'$ is pointwise bounded; by the Banach--Steinhaus uniform boundedness 
principle~\cite[Theorem~3.5.4]{BSS2017tvs}, it is norm-bounded, i.e., $A$ is norm-bounded.

By the Hahn--Banach theorem, 
$$
B(n)=\bigcap\{\{x:|\varphi(x)|\le n\}:\varphi\in E',\ \|\varphi\|\le 1\},
$$ 
so that 
$B(n)$ is closed in $E_w$. Consequently, the family $\mathscr B$ consists of closed precompact subsets of $E_w$. 
Moreover, any convergent sequence in $E_w$ is bounded in $E_w$ and hence norm-bounded, which implies that the 
family $\mathscr B$ absorbs convergent sequences in~$E_w$.
head: environment

label: prop:bs-kfu-baire-sgs
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:bs-kfu-baire-sgs}
Let $E$ be a normed space, and let $\tau$ be a vector space topology on $E$ between the topologies of $E$ and $E_w$.
 If $G$ is a $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn or Baire subgroup of the space $(E,\tau)$, then the topology of $G$ 
coincides with the topology induced from~$E$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:bs-as} and Remark~\ref{rem:finer} the family $\mathscr B=\{B(n): n\in \omega\}$ consists of closed 
subsets of $(E,\tau)$ and absorbs convergent sequences in $(E,\tau)$.

If $G$ is $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn, then the 
topology of $G$ coincides with that induced from $E$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:kfu-group-tvs}(ii).

If $G$ is Baire, then  the topology of $G$ coincides 
with that induced from $E$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:sg-baire-tvs}(ii).
head: environment

label: th:bs-kfu-baire-sgs
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
According to Lemma~\ref{lemma:bs-as}, the family $\mathscr B=\{B(n): n\in \omega\}$ consists of closed 
precompact subsets of $E_w$ and absorbs convergent sequences in $E_w$.

If $G$ is 
$\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn, then it is locally precompact by 
Proposition~\ref{prop:kfu-group-loc-precomp} and hence locally finite-dimensional by 
Theorem~\ref{th:lfd-subgroups}. If $G$ is Baire, then it is locally finite-dimensional 
by Proposition~\ref{prop:sg-baire-tvs}(iii). 

Alternatively, the theorem follows directly from Theorem~\ref{th:criterion}, because, by 
Lemma~\ref{lemma:bs-as}, the norm of $E$ satisfies conditions (a)--(c) on $E_w$.
head: environment

label: cor:bs-kfu-baire-sgs
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Remark
head: environment

label: q:cont-norm
title: Question
body_md:
\label{q:cont-norm}
Let $V$ be a locally convex space admitting a continuous norm. Is every $\varkappa$-Fr\'echet--Urysohn 
\textup(Fr\'echet--Urysohn, metrizable\textup) subgroup of $V_w$ locally finite-dimensional? Is every 
$\varkappa$-Fr\'echet--Urysohn linear subspace of $V_w$ finite-dimensional?
head: environment

label: lemma:weakstar
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) This is the classical Banach--Alaoglu theorem.

(ii) Let $K\subset E'$ be weak$^*$ compact. For every $x\in E$, the map $\varphi\mapsto\varphi(x)$ is continuous 
on $E'_{w^*}$; hence the set $\{\varphi(x):\varphi\in K\}$ is compact and therefore bounded. Since $E$ is complete, 
the Banach--Steinhaus uniform boundedness principle~\cite[Theorem~3.5.4]{BSS2017tvs} applied to the family $K$ 
of continuous linear functionals on~$E$ shows that $\sup\{\|\varphi\|:\varphi\in K\}<\infty$. 

The last assertion holds because a convergent sequence together with its limit is compact.
head: environment

label: rem:hemicompact-ref
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:hemicompact-ref}
Apparently, the hemicompactness of $E'_{w^*}$ is folklore; it is stated without proof in \cite[Example~1.3(c)]{KampoukosMercourakis2013}.
As we have mentioned before, the fact that, for any infinite-dimensional Banach space $E$, the spaces $E_w$ and $E'_{w^*}$ are
not $k$-spaces is well known \cite{KM2017}.
head: environment

label: th:weakstar
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $G$ be a $\varkappa$-Fr\'echet--Urysohn subgroup of $E'_{w^*}$. By Proposition~\ref{lemma:weakstar} and 
Corollary~\ref{cor:hemicompact-group}, the set $G\cap B(n)$ is a neighborhood of zero in $G$ for some $n$. This 
set is precompact in $G$, because $B(n)$ is compact and hence precompact in $E'_{w^*}$ (see 
Section~\ref{Preliminaries}). Therefore, $G$ is locally precompact and, by Theorem~\ref{th:lfd-subgroups}, 
locally finite-dimensional.

If $G$ is a Baire subgroup of $E'_{w^*}$, then $G$ is locally finite-dimensional by 
Proposition~\ref{prop:sg-baire-tvs}(iii), because the balls $B(r)$ are compact and hence closed and precompact 
in $E'_{w^*}$.

Alternatively, the theorem follows from Theorem~\ref{th:criterion}, because, by 
Proposition~\ref{lemma:weakstar}, the dual norm satisfies conditions (a)--(c) of that theorem.
head: environment

label: ex:incomplete
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:incomplete}
Let $E$ be any normed space of countably infinite \textup(Hamel\textup) dimension. If 
 $\{e_k:k\in\omega\}$ is a Hamel 
basis of $E$, then the weak$^*$ topology is generated by the countably many functionals 
$\varphi\mapsto\varphi(e_k)$, and hence $E'_{w^*}$ is an infinite-dimensional metrizable TVS.
head: environment

label: rem:normed-dual
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:normed-dual}
For an arbitrary normed space $E$, the balls $B(n)$ are still compact in $E'_{w^*}$ by the Banach--Alaoglu theorem, 
which holds for normed spaces; thus, conditions (a) and (c) of Theorem~\ref{th:criterion} are satisfied. Therefore, 
by Proposition~\ref{prop:sg-baire-tvs}(iii), \emph{every Baire subgroup of $E'_{w^*}$ is locally finite-dimensional 
for any normed space $E$}; only the $\varkappa$-Fr\'echet--Urysohn part of Theorem~\ref{th:weakstar} requires 
condition~(b). In Example~\ref{ex:incomplete}, the space $E'_{w^*}=\bigcup_n B(n)$ is indeed not Baire.
head: environment

label: prop:lbx-bounded
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:lbx-bounded}
For any space $X$, the following assertions hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm (i)]
$\|\chi\|=\sup\{|\chi(f)|: f\in C_b(X),\ \|f\|_\infty\le 1\}$ for every $\chi\in E(X)$.
\item[\rm (ii)]
For any $r\ge 0$, the ball $B_r(X)=\{\chi\in E(X):\|\chi\|\le r\}$ is closed in $L_b(X)$.
\item[\rm (iii)]
A set $B\subset L_b(X)$ is bounded in $L_b(X)$ if and only if there exists an $n\in \omega$ 
for which $B\subset B_n(X)$. 
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) Clearly, $|\chi(f)|\le\|\chi\|\,\|f\|_\infty$. Conversely, let $\chi=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_ix_i$, where the 
$x_i$ are distinct and $\lambda_i\ne0$. Take pairwise disjoint open sets $O_i\ni x_i$ and continuous functions 
$g_i\colon X\to[0,1]$  such that $g_i(x_i)=1$ and $g_i=0$ outside $O_i$. Then 
$f=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{sign}(\lambda_i)\,g_i\in C_b(X)$, $\|f\|_\infty\le1$, and $\chi(f)=\|\chi\|$.

(ii) By (i), the function $\chi\mapsto\|\chi\|$ is the supremum of a family of continuous functions on 
$L_b(X)$ and hence is lower semicontinuous.

(iii) By (i), the map $J\colon E(X)\to C_b(X)'$  defined by $J(\chi)(f)=\chi(f)$ 
is a linear isometry of $(E(X),\lVert\boldsymbol\cdot\rVert)$ into the dual of the Banach space $(C_b(X),\lVert\boldsymbol\cdot\rVert_\infty)$.
If $B$ is bounded in $L_b(X)$, then the set $\{\chi(f): \chi\in B\}$ is
bounded for every $f\in C_b(X)$. It follows from the Banach--Steinhaus uniform boundedness principle
\cite[Theorem~3.5.4]{BSS2017tvs} that $J(B)$ is norm-bounded in $C_b(X)'$, i.e., 
$B\subset B_n(X)$ for some $n$. 
Conversely, if $B\subset B_n(X)$, then $|\chi(f)|\le n\|f\|_\infty$ for all $\chi\in B$ and $f\in C_b(X)$; 
hence $B$ is bounded in the locally convex space $L_b(X)$.
head: environment

label: p6
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p6}
For any space $X$, the family of $B_n(X)$, $n\in \omega$, consists of closed subsets of $L_b(X)$ and 
absorbs convergent sequences in $L_b(X)$ \textup(and therefore in $L_p(X)$, $L(X)$, $V(X)$, and $E(X)$ with any 
vector space topology finer than that of $L_b(X)$\textup).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:lbx-bounded}, because any convergent sequence is bounded, and 
from Remark~\ref{rem:finer}.
head: environment

label: lemma:En-closed
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\chi\in E(X)\setminus E_n(X)$, and let $x_0,\dots,x_n$ be distinct points of $\operatorname{supp}\chi$. 
Take pairwise disjoint open sets $O_i\ni x_i$ such that $O_i\cap\operatorname{supp}\chi=\{x_i\}$ and continuous functions 
$g_i\colon X\to[0,1]$ with $g_i(x_i)=1$ and $g_i=0$ outside $O_i$, $i=0,\dots,n$. Then $\chi(g_i)\ne0$ for 
all $i$ and the set $W=\{\eta\in E(X):\eta(g_i)\ne0,\ i=0,\dots,n\}$ is an open neighborhood of $\chi$ in 
$L_b(X)$. If $\eta\in W$, then $\operatorname{supp}\eta$ meets each of the $n+1$ disjoint sets $O_i$, so that 
$|\operatorname{supp}\eta|>n$. Thus, $W\cap E_n(X)=\varnothing$.
head: environment

label: c3
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{c3}
Let $X$ be any topological space, and let $V$ be $E(X)$ endowed with any vector space topology finer than that 
of $L_b(X)$. Then the topology of any $\varkappa$-Fr\'echet--Urysohn subgroup of $V$ is finer than that 
induced by the norm~$\lVert\boldsymbol\cdot\rVert$.
head: environment

label: p7
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p7}
For any topological space $X$, the family $\{E_n(X): n\in \omega\}$ absorbs convergent sequences in $V(X)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\xi=(\chi_n)_{n\in\omega}$ be a convergent sequence in $V(X)$, and let $V(X,\beta X)$ denote the subspace 
of $V(\beta X)$ generated by $X$; clearly, $V(X,\beta X)$ and $V(X)$ coincide as sets, the topology of $V(X)$ 
is finer than that of $V(X,\beta X)$, and $\xi$ remains a convergent 
sequence in $V(X,\beta X)$.
We set 
$$
F_n=E_n(\beta X)\cap B_n(\beta X)=\Bigl\{\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i x_i: x_i\in \beta X, 
\lambda_i\in \mathbb R, \sum_{i=1}^n|\lambda_i|\le n\Bigr\}
$$
for $n\in \omega$ (some of the $\lambda_i$ may vanish). 
Note that each $F_n$ is a continuous image of the space 
$$
(\beta X)^n\times K,\quad\text{where }K=\{(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)\in \mathbb R^n: |\lambda_1|+\dots+|\lambda_n|\le n\}.
$$
Since $K$ is a closed subset of the compact space $[-n,n]^n$, it follows that every $F_n$ is compact. 
Note also that $F_{n}\subset F_{n+1}$ and 
$V(\beta X)$ is the inductive limit of the sequence $(F_n)_{n\in\omega}$ 
\cite[Theorem~3.1]{GM2017ftvs}. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:ind-limit} and Remark~\ref{rem:finer}, 
$\xi\subset F_n\cap E(X)\subset E_n(X)$ for some~$n\in\omega$.

label: lemma:lfd
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
$(\Rightarrow)$
Suppose that $G$ is locally finite-dimensional. Then $G\cap L$ is open in $G$ for some finite-dimensional 
subspace $L\subset E(X)$. We have  $L\subset E(M)$ for a finite $M\subset X$. Let $n=|M|$. 
Then $G\cap L\subset E_{n}(X)$ and, consequently, $G\cap E_n(X)$ has nonempty interior in~$G$.

$(\Leftarrow)$
Suppose that $G\cap E_n(X)$ has nonempty interior in $G$ for some $n\in \omega$.
If $g+O\subset E_n(X)$, where $g\in G$ and $O$ is a neighborhood of zero in $G$, then 
$O\subset E_n(X)-g\subset E_{2n}(X)$. Thus, $G\cap E_{2n}(X)$ is a neighborhood of zero in $G$. Let $U\subset G$ be a neighborhood of zero of $G$ such 
that $U+\dots+U\subset E_{2n}(X)$ ($2n+1$ summands).

The subgroup $\langle U\rangle$ is open in $G$, and $\langle U\rangle\subset E(S)$, where $S=\operatorname{supp} U$. Therefore, it suffices to 
prove that $S$ is finite: then $E(S)$ is a finite-dimensional subspace and $G\cap E(S)\supset\langle U\rangle$ is open 
in~$G$. Suppose that $S$ is infinite. 
Then the following claim holds.

\smallskip
\noindent
{\bf Claim 1.} 
{\it
 There exist $\chi_i \in U$ and $x_i\in X$, $i=1,\dots,2n+1$, such that
$x_i\in \operatorname{supp} \chi_i \setminus \bigcup_{j\ne i} \operatorname{supp}\chi_j$ for each~$i$. 
}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Claim 1]
Since $S$ is infinite and all supports are finite, the family $\{\operatorname{supp} \chi:\chi\in U\}$ is 
infinite; each of its members  has at most $2n$ elements.  
Corollary~\ref{cor:Delta-system} and Remark~\ref{rem:delta}  imply the 
existence of a $Y\subset X$ and a family $\{\chi_i:i\in \omega\}\subset U$ such that the sequence $\{\operatorname{supp}\chi_i:i\in \omega\}$ consists of distinct 
elements, $\operatorname{supp}\chi_i\setminus Y\ne\varnothing$, and $\operatorname{supp}\chi_i\cap \operatorname{supp}\chi_j=Y$ for distinct $i,j\in \omega$. We take 
$x_i\in \operatorname{supp} \chi_i \setminus Y$ for $i=1,\dots,2n+1$. 
\end{proof}

We set 
\[
\chi = \sum_{i=1}^{2n+1} \chi_i.
\]
Note that $\{x_1, \dots, x_{2n+1}\}\subset \operatorname{supp} \chi$. Indeed, 
suppose that $x_i\notin \operatorname{supp} \chi$. Then $\chi\in E(X\setminus \{x_i\})$. Since 
$x_i\notin \operatorname{supp} \chi_j$ for $j\ne i$, we also have $\chi_j\in E(X\setminus \{x_i\})$ for 
$j\ne i$. Therefore, 
$$
\chi_i=\chi-\sum_{j\ne i}\chi_j \in E(X\setminus \{x_i\}), 
$$
which contradicts the fact that $x_i\in \operatorname{supp} \chi_i$. 

Thus, $|\operatorname{supp} \chi|>2n$ and, consequently, $\chi\notin E_{2n}(X)$. On the other hand, 
$\chi\in U+\dots+U \subset E_{2n}(X)$. This contradiction proves the lemma.

title: Proof
body_md:
The sets $E_n(X)$ are closed in $L_b(X)$ (by Lemma~\ref{lemma:En-closed}) and hence in $(E(X), \tau)$.
Since $G$ is Baire and $G=\bigcup_{n\in\omega} E_n(X)\cap G$, it follows that the interior of $E_n(X)\cap G$ 
in $G$ is nonempty for some~$n$.
Lemma~\ref{lemma:lfd} implies that $G$ is locally finite-dimensional.

label: lemma:lpx-bounded
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:lpx-bounded}
For any space $X$ and any bounded set $B\subset L_p(X)$, 
the set $\operatorname{supp} B=\bigcup_{\chi\in B} \operatorname{supp} \chi$ is functionally bounded 
in~$X$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $\operatorname{supp} B$ is not functionally bounded. Then there exists a discrete family $\{U_n:n\in\omega\}$ of open sets such that 
$U_n\cap \operatorname{supp} B\neq \varnothing$ for $n\in \omega$. For each $n\in\omega$, take $\chi_n\in B$ such that $\operatorname{supp} \chi_n\cap 
U_n\neq\varnothing$. Since every $\operatorname{supp}\chi_n$ is finite and meets only finitely many members of the discrete family 
$\{U_n\}$, there exists a subsequence $(\chi_{n_k})_{k\in\omega}$ such that 
$U_{n_k} \cap \operatorname{supp} \chi_{n_i}= \varnothing$ for $i<k<\omega$; clearly, the $\chi_{n_k}$ are pairwise 
distinct.

For each $k\in \omega$, we set $\xi_k=\chi_{n_k}$ and choose $x_k\in \operatorname{supp} \xi_k$ and a neighborhood $V_k$ of $x_k$ 
so that $x_k\in V_k\subset U_{n_k}$ and $\{x_k\}=V_k\cap \operatorname{supp} \xi_k$. 
Let $f_k\colon X\to [0,1]$ be a continuous function such that $f_k(x_k)=1$ and $f_k^{-1}((0,1])\subset V_k$. 
Then $\xi_k(f_k)\neq 0$ and $V_k\cap \operatorname{supp} \xi_i=\varnothing$ for $i<k$; hence $\xi_i(f_k)=0$ for $i<k$.

We define $\lambda_k\in \mathbb{R}$ by induction on $k \in \omega$ as follows. 
We set $\lambda_0=1$. Assuming that $k>0$ and $\lambda_0, \dots, \lambda_{k-1}$ are already defined, 
we consider $c=\xi_k\bigl(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\lambda_i f_i\bigr)$ and choose $\lambda_k\in \mathbb{R}$ so that 
$\lambda_k\xi_k(f_k)+c>k$; it exists because $\xi_k(f_k)\neq 0$. 

We have 
\[
\xi_k\biggl(\sum_{i=0}^{k}\lambda_i f_i\biggr)>k.
\]
Let $f=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\lambda_i f_i$. Since the family $\{V_i\}$ is discrete, this sum is locally 
finite; therefore, the function $f$ is continuous. Since $\xi_k(f_i)=0$ for $i>k$, we have 
$\xi_k(f)=\xi_k\bigl(\sum_{i=0}^{k}\lambda_i f_i\bigr)>k$ for $k\in\omega$.
This contradicts the boundedness of the set~$B$.
head: environment

label: t4
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $G$ be a $\varkappa$-Fr\'echet--Urysohn subgroup of $E=(E(X), \tau)$.
From Corollary \ref{c3} it follows that the topology of $G$ is finer than the topology generated 
by~$\lVert\boldsymbol\cdot\rVert$.

\smallskip
\noindent
{\bf Claim 2.}
{\it
If $\xi=(v_n)_n\subset G$ is a sequence convergent in $G$, then the set $\operatorname{supp} \xi=\bigcup_{n\in\omega} \operatorname{supp} v_n$ is 
finite.}
 
\begin{proof}[Proof of Claim 2] 
Let $v$ be the limit of the sequence $\xi$.  We can assume that $v=0$, because 
$\operatorname{supp} v_n\subset \operatorname{supp}(v_n-v)\cup\operatorname{supp} v$ and $(v_n-v)_n$ is a 
sequence in $G$ converging to zero.
Since $\xi$ is a convergent sequence in $L_p(X)$ and hence bounded, it follows by Lemma~\ref{lemma:lpx-bounded} that 
$M=\operatorname{supp} \xi$ is a functionally bounded subset 
of $X$. Let $H=\langle \xi \rangle$ (the subgroup of $G$ generated by $\xi$; note that $H\subset E(M)$), 
and let $\widetilde H$ be the closure of $H$ in the completion 
$\widehat E$ of $E$.

We show that $\widetilde H$ is locally compact.
Since $M$ is functionally bounded in $X$ and hence in $L(X)$, it follows that $M$ is precompact 
in $L(X)$ (see, e.g., \cite[Lemma~2.9]{Gab_Schur}). Therefore, so is  its absolutely convex hull 
$D=E(M)\cap B_1(X)$ \cite[Proposition~1.8.2]{BSS2017tvs}.
Since the topology of $L(X)$ is finer than  that of $E$, the closure 
$\widetilde D$ of $D$ in $\widehat E$ is compact. Note that $B_1(X)\cap G$ is a neighborhood of zero in $G$, 
since  the topology of $G$ is finer than the norm topology generated by $\lVert\boldsymbol\cdot\rVert$. 
Therefore, $\widetilde D\cap \widetilde H$ is a compact neighborhood of zero in 
$\widetilde H$, because $B_1(X)\cap H$ is a neighborhood 
of zero in $H$, its closure in $\widetilde H$ is a neighborhood of zero in $\widetilde H$ ($H$ is dense 
in $\widetilde H$), and $B_1(X)\cap H\subset D$. Thus, $\widetilde H$ is locally compact.

Theorem~\ref{th:lc-subgroups} (applied  to the TVS $\widehat E$) implies that 
$\widetilde H$ is locally finite-di\-men\-sion\-al. Consequently, $H$ is locally finite-dimensional 
(by Remark~\ref{rem1}; see also the end of the proof of Theorem~\ref{th:lfd-subgroups}). Hence there exists a 
finite $S\subset X$ such that $H\cap E(S)$ is a neighborhood of zero in $H$.
Since $v_i\to0$ in $H$, there exists an $n\in\omega$ for which $\operatorname{supp} v_i\subset S$ for $i>n$.
Therefore, $M\subset S\cup \bigcup_{i\leq n}\operatorname{supp} v_i$ and hence $M$ is finite.
This completes the proof of Claim~2.
\end{proof}

\smallskip

Suppose that $G$ is not locally finite-dimensional.
Then, for any finite $M\subset X$, the set $G\cap E(M)$ is closed (because $E(M)$ is 
finite-dimensional) and nowhere dense in $G$ (otherwise, the subgroup $G\cap E(M)$ would be open in 
$G$). Since $G$ 
is $\varkappa$-Fr\'echet--Urysohn and $0\in\overline{G\setminus E(M)}$, there exists a sequence 
$\xi_M\subset G\setminus E(M)$ converging to zero. Note that $\operatorname{supp}\xi_M$ is finite by Claim~2.

Let us construct by induction on $n$ an increasing sequence $(M_n)_n$ of finite subsets of $X$ 
and a sequence $(\xi_n)_n$ of sequences converging to zero satisfying the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $M_0=\varnothing$;
\item[(b)] $\operatorname{supp} \xi_i\subset M_n$ for $i<n$;
\item[(c)] $\xi_n\subset G\setminus E(M_n)$.
\end{enumerate}

\emph{Base case}.\enspace We set $M_0=\varnothing$ and $\xi_0=\xi_\varnothing$.

\emph{Induction step}.\enspace  For $n>0$, we set $M_n=M_{n-1}\cup \operatorname{supp} \xi_{n-1}$ and $\xi_n=\xi_{M_n}$. 

Suppose that $\xi_n=(v_{ni})_i$. For $i\in\omega$, let $r_{ni}>0$ be the minimum of the absolute values of 
the (nonzero) coefficients of $v_{ni}$, and let 
$U_{ni}=\{v\in G:\|v-v_{ni}\|<r_{ni}\}$. By Corollary~\ref{c3} the set $U_{ni}$ is open in $G$. 
If $v\in U_{ni}$, then $\operatorname{supp} v_{ni}\subset \operatorname{supp} v$: otherwise, for $s\in \operatorname{supp} v_{ni}\setminus\operatorname{supp} v$, 
the coefficient of $s$ in $v-v_{ni}$ has absolute value at least $r_{ni}$. Let $U_n=\bigcup_{i\in \omega}U_{ni}$.
Then $0\in \overline{U_n}$, because $v_{ni}\to0$ as $i\to\infty$. Moreover, 
$\operatorname{supp} u \cap (M_{n+1}\setminus M_n) \neq \varnothing$ for $u\in U_n$, because 
$\operatorname{supp} v_{ni}\subset M_{n+1}$ by (b) and $\operatorname{supp} v_{ni}\not\subset M_n$ by~(c).

Theorem \ref{t1} implies that $G$ is strongly $\varkappa$-Fr\'echet--Urysohn.
By Proposition~\ref{p1} there exist a sequence $(u_k)_k$ converging to zero and a strictly increasing 
sequence $(n_k)_k$ of nonnegative integers such that $u_k\in U_{n_k}$. Since $\operatorname{supp} u_k \cap (M_{n_k+1}\setminus M_{n_k}) \neq \varnothing$ 
for $k\in\omega$ and the sets $M_{n+1}\setminus M_n$ are pairwise disjoint, 
it follows that the set $\operatorname{supp} (u_k)_k$ is infinite in contradiction to Claim~2.
This completes the proof.

This completes the proof of Claim~2.

label: cor:lbx-kfu
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:lbx-kfu}
For any topological space $X$, every $\varkappa$-Fr\'echet--Urysohn subgroup of $L_b(X)$ is locally finite-dimensional.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the map $J$ from $(E(X),\lVert\boldsymbol\cdot\rVert)$ to the dual of the Banach space $(C_b(X),\lVert\boldsymbol\cdot\rVert_\infty)$
defined by the rule $J(\chi) = (f\mapsto\chi(f))$.
By Proposition~\ref{prop:lbx-bounded} $J$ is a linear isometry, and, by definition, the topology of $L_b(X)$ 
is induced by the weak$^*$ topology of $C_b(X)'$. Thus, $L_b(X)$ is a linear subspace of $(C_b(X))'_{w^*}$, and it 
remains to apply Theorem~\ref{th:weakstar}. (Alternatively, one can apply Theorem~\ref{t4} to $\beta X$, because 
$L_b(X)$ is a linear subspace of $L_p(\beta X)$.)
head: environment

label: th:VX-kfu
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th:VX-kfu}
For any topological space $X$, every $\varkappa$-Fr\'echet--Urysohn subgroup of $V(X)$ is locally finite-dimensional.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It follows from Proposition~\ref{p7} that the family $\{E_n(X): n\in \omega\}$ absorbs convergent sequences in $V(X)$.
Let $G$ be a $\varkappa$-Fr\'echet--Urysohn subgroup of $V(X)$. 
Then the family  $\{F_n=G\cap E_n(X):n\in \omega\}$ absorbs convergent sequences in $G$.
The sets $F_n$ are closed in $G$ (by Lemma~\ref{lemma:En-closed}) and the sequence of $F_n$ is increasing.
It follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:kfu-group-as} that $G\cap E_n(X)$ is a neighborhood of zero in $G$ for some $n\in \omega$.
Lemma \ref{lemma:lfd} implies that $G$ is locally finite-dimensional.
head: environment

label: th:lss-baire
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th:lss-baire}
Let $\tau$ be a vector space topology on $E(X)$ finer than the topology of $L_b(X)$. Then any Baire linear subspace of $(E(X), \tau)$ is finite-dimensional.
head: environment

label: th:lss-kfu
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: ex:norm
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:norm}
Let $X$ be an infinite compact space. Recall that for every $\chi=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i x_i \in E(X)$ the norm $\|\chi\|=\sum_{i=1}^n |\lambda_i|$
has been defined. Let $\tau_1$ be the topology on $E(X)$ generated by this norm 
$\lVert\boldsymbol\cdot\rVert$. Since $|\chi(f)|\le\|\chi\|\,\|f\|_\infty$ and all continuous functions on $X$ are bounded, $\tau_1$ is 
finer than the topology of $L_p(X)=L_b(X)$. The space $(E(X),\tau_1)$ is metrizable and infinite-dimensional, 
so that it is a Fr\'echet--Urysohn (and hence $\varkappa$-Fr\'echet--Urysohn) linear subspace of itself which is 
not finite-dimensional. Note that $\tau_1$ is not coarser than the topology of $L(X)$, because 
$\|x-y\|=2$ for distinct $x,y\in X$ and $X$ is not discrete. (Of course, $(E(X),\tau_1)$ is not Baire by virtue of Theorem~\ref{th:lss-baire}.)
